newsitem.title: USA: Blood-cell drug benefits limited - studies.
newsitem.headline: Blood-cell drug benefits limited - studies.

text.p: A hormone designed to boost disease-fighting white blood cells may achieve that objective, but offers few significant benefits to patients, according to two studies in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

The hormone known as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, or G-CSF, helps counteract neutropenia, a dangerous reduction in one type of disease-fighting white blood cell. It is sold under the brand name Neupogen by Amgen Inc. of Thousand Oaks, Calif.

In the first study, a group led by Dr. Lynn C. Hartmann of the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minn., gave either G-CSF or a placebo to 138 people whose white blood cell count had declined because they were taking anti-cancer drugs.
G-CSF raised the blood cell count back up, they found, but it did not reduce the risk of hospital treatment, shorten hospital stays or decrease the number of infections a person suffered.
Hartmann and her colleagues concluded the hormone "has little practical clinical benefit."
The second study involved 164 children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, half of whom received the hormone to treat their neutropenia.

Conducted at the St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and the University of Tennessee, this study also found the hormone did not reduce the risk of hospitalization, increase the survival rate among the children, or save money.
It did, however, get the children out of the hospital faster and seemed to prevent a number of infections, they said.

The St. Jude team, led by Dr. Ching-Hon Pui, said G-CSF "had some clinical benefit in children," but it did not reduce the rate of hospitalization, "prolong survival, or reduce the cost of supportive care."
"At St. Jude, we now believe that G-CSF should be used selectively, not routinely, in these patients."
The Pui team did not find any evidence that the G-CSF treatments stimulated the cancerous growth of other blood cells, which has been a lingering fear about the treatment.
